articles.title: US Warns Of Ongoing Cyber Threat To Industrial Freezers And Cold Storage
articles.description: US Warns Of Ongoing Cyber Threat To Industrial Freezers And Cold Storage Authored by Kimberly Hayek via The Epoch Times, Federal agencies warned Thursday that hackers are targeting refrigeration systems used to store food and medicine, urging businesses to secure vulnerable controls amid attacks that could spoil supplies and damage equipment. The Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA), the FBI, and the departments of Health and Human Services and Agriculture and Transportation described the ongoing malicious activity as targeting unpatched or internet-accessible temperature and commercial refrigeration controllers. The systems are widely used in healthcare, chemical, food and agriculture, and transportation operations. In a fact sheet, officials said successful attacks could allow hackers to alter temperatures, force units into continuous heating or defrost cycles, and create risks including inventory loss, equipment damage, and potential fire hazards. "Every organization that depends on refrigeration and monitoring systems should assume it could be a target," Chris Butera, CISA's acting executive assistant director for cybersecurity, said in a statement. He urged operators to review the guidance and close known security gaps. FBI Cyber Branch Operations Director Brett Leatherman said the agency is seeing the systems targeted across critical infrastructure sectors globally. "These systems protect food, medicine and other temperature-sensitive products, making them attractive targets," he said. The FBI encouraged organizations to implement the recommended mitigations and report suspicious activity. The agencies recommended that operators remove control systems from the public internet, change default and weak passwords, apply available patches, replace unsupported legacy devices, and limit or secure any necessary remote access. Hackers Hit European Supermarkets The warning follows a series of reported attacks on supermarket refrigeration systems in Europe. On Monday, supermarket chains in Belgium, Ireland, Sweden, and other European countries reported that freezers and refrigerators had been remotely set to high temperatures. Irish wholesaler Musgrave said a cyber incident affected refrigeration units in 13 SuperValu stores, forcing them to remove some chilled and frozen products. Belgian and Luxembourg operators Delhaize and Colruyt, along with Carrefour, also reported impacts at multiple locations. In Stockholm, an ICA store manager said that freezers reached 50 degrees Celsius (122 degrees Fahrenheit) after an overnight attack that went undetected for hours. A Selver supermarket in Estonia was similarly affected. Defrost Mode Triggered The incidents follow a larger wave of attacks in France last month, in which refrigeration systems at hundreds of stores were reportedly forced into defrost mode for hours. One French chain estimated losses in the tens of millions of euros from a single day's disruption. French Finance Minister Roland Lescure said roughly 700 of the country's 10,000 supermarkets were affected and described the incident as a wake-up call for food security. A separate cyberattack on Monday targeted refrigeration systems at three sites of France's public blood service, forcing temperatures to rise in cold storage rooms. Officials said monitoring and alarm systems allowed rapid response, and no blood products were compromised. U.S. officials did not attribute the European incidents to any specific group or confirm whether they have detected similar attacks inside the United States. Reuters contributed to this report. Tyler Durden Sun, 11/08/2026 - 21:35

articles.title: Police flag the use of AI by criminals
articles.description: Police are warning that more criminals are making use of artificial intelligence to carry out technology-related crimes, leading to a rise in ransomware cases in the first three quarters of this year. The number of these kinds of cases rose by 18 percent year-on-year to 40 during the period. Despite this, there was an overall dip of 12 percent in the number of tech crimes to 21,573 cases, along with a 15 percent drop in total losses that stood at almost HK$3.9 billion. Chief Superintendent Raymond Lam from the Cyber Security and Technology Crime Bureau noted that agentic AI – autonomous AI systems that execute tasks with minimal human supervision – was widely adopted by criminals to path the attack kill chains in order to carry out hack attacks. "They may be used in that kind of cyberattack, like system scanning, vulnerability scanning, penetration, etc," he said. "Indeed, we understand that the use of AI, they obviously increased the speed of attack, the volume, and the intrusiveness, so that the attack will be more effective." Police officials believe criminals have scaled up their reconnaissance and phishing attacks before initiating ransomware attacks using AI. The growing trend highlighted the importance of Hong Kong police collaborating with both mainland authorities and Interpol, as the rapid evolution of AI poses a challenge to law enforcement. To meet the challenge, the SAR joined Interpol’s first year-long AI-powered cyber operation targeting potential phishing and fraudulent links. Using an AI-analysis engine, created by Hong Kong police, which can analyse a website’s features, such as its domain and the technical infrastructure, officers can take down or block sites that are deemed risky, before the links reach more people. Enrique Hernandez-Gonzalez, Assistant Director of Cybercrime Operations at Interpol’s Cybercrime Directorate said such intelligence was shared with 47 jurisdictions. As a result, among the roughly 57,000 links that were investigated in the campaign, about 90 percent of them have become inaccessible. “Hong Kong has information about malicious domains or victims that may be located in other countries,” he said. “Using Interpol’s channel, we put that information in the outlets of these countries, so they can take action.” The second phase of the operation – featuring the involvement of more than 20 jurisdictions across five continents – was launched last month. Edited by Tony Sabine
